lessons.title: 2.1 Introduction: why do we need files?

blocks.html: Every variable in a program lives in RAM. RAM is volatile: when the program ends or the power goes off, everything in it is lost. Imagine a school marks program where the teacher types the marks of 60 students, closes the program, and finds next morning that everything is gone.

A file is a named collection of data stored on a secondary storage device such as a hard disk, SSD or pen drive. Data in a file stays there after the program ends, so the program can read it again later.

blocks.html: In C++, all input and output happens through streams. A stream is a flow of bytes between the program and a device. You already use two streams: cin (keyboard to program) and cout (program to screen). File handling uses the same idea, but the device is a file on the disk.

blocks.caption: Figure 2.2 · streams connect the program to devices and files

blocks.html: To work with files, include the header <fstream> . It gives three classes.
These classes are derived from ostream , istream and iostream . That is why the same operators << and >> that you use with cout and cin also work with files.
There are two ways to open a file.

blocks.code: ofstream fout("marks.txt");          // opens marks.txt for writing

ofstream fout;
fout.open("marks.txt");
fout.close();

blocks.html: Closing a file flushes the buffer. Data waiting in memory is actually written to the disk, and the file is released for other programs. The stream's destructor also closes the file automatically (RAII, Chapter 1), but it is good practice to call close() yourself.
A file may fail to open: it may not exist, the name may be wrong, or the folder may be read- only. Always check.

lessons.title: 2.5 File pointers: moving inside a file

blocks.html: Every open file has two position markers, called file pointers:

items.html: get pointer: where the next read will happen (moved by seekg , "g" for get)
put pointer: where the next write will happen (moved by seekp , "p" for put)

blocks.html: The position is counted in bytes from the start, beginning at 0.

blocks.text: 2.5.1 Example: find the size of a file

blocks.html: Without clear() , the stream stays in the end-of-file state, and the second loop reads nothing.
In Python, the pickle module is used to save objects. In C++, a structure or object is written byte for byte with write() and read back with read() .

blocks.code:
fout.write((char*)&obj, sizeof(obj));   // memory -> file
fin.read((char*)&obj, sizeof(obj));     // file -> memory

items.html: (char*)&obj gives the address of the object, seen as a series of bytes.
sizeof(obj) tells how many bytes to copy.
Every record has the same size, so record number n (counting from 1) starts at byte

blocks.html: (n - 1) * sizeof(obj) . This makes it possible to jump straight to any record.

Important rule: Inside a structure written to a binary file, use char arrays (char name[30] ) and not std::string . A string keeps its text somewhere else in memory, so writing it with write() saves only an address, not the text.

blocks.text: Group activity: Where do apps store data? (10 minutes)

blocks.html: In groups, choose an app (WhatsApp, a railway ticket app, a hospital billing system). Discuss what data it must keep permanently, whether a text file or a binary file suits each kind of data, and why big apps finally move to databases (Chapter 8).

items.html: Data in variables (RAM) is lost when a program ends. Files store data permanently on a disk.
Text files store readable characters. Binary files store the exact bytes from memory, so they are smaller and faster.
Include <fstream> . Use ofstream to write, ifstream to read, and fstream to do both.
